title: Iran Struck a Qatari State LNG Tanker in the Authorized Corridor — With Its Transponder Off
narrative:
On July 7, 2026, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps fired at least two missiles at commercial vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz — striking the Qatari liquefied natural gas tanker Al Rekayyat and a Saudi-flagged crude oil supertanker, the Wedyan. The Al Rekayyat is owned and managed by Nakilat, Qatar's state-owned shipping arm and the operator of the world's largest LNG fleet. It was struck on its port side at the top of the engine room while traveling without its transponders active, ship-tracking data from MarineTraffic shows. The vessel had loaded cargo at Qatar's Ras Laffan facility — the world's largest LNG export terminal — hours before the strike. European gas prices climbed 4.1 percent on the news. Qatar's foreign ministry called the strike "an unacceptable attack on the security of international navigation" and demanded Iran cease actions threatening regional stability.

The attacks came 72 hours after Khamenei's body completed its six-day funeral procession, as the IRGC sent maritime radio warnings over the weekend: "Our missiles and drones are ready to fire at you," according to a recording obtained by the Wall Street Journal. The strikes violate the June MOU under which Iran agreed to halt attacks on commercial shipping. Only three vessels sailed with transponders on through the US-managed Omani corridor on Monday — the rest traveled dark, and still two were hit.

The OSINT contradiction at the center of this strike is the transponder-off passage through the authorized corridor. Both the June MOU and IRGC's own maritime radio warning specified that vessels following the US-authorized Omani corridor would be safe. The Al Rekayyat was on that corridor and was dark — a common practice to avoid targeting — and still struck. This means either Iran has surveillance coverage of the entire corridor including dark ships, defeating the "authorized route" premise, or Iran struck a known Qatari state vessel deliberately, not a random targeting error.

The Al Rekayyat transponder-off passage is the primary OSINT contradiction. Both the June MOU and the IRGC's weekend radio warning specified that vessels following the US-authorized Omani corridor would be safe. The Al Rekayyat was on that corridor and was dark — a common practice to avoid targeting — and still struck. This means either (a) Iran has surveillance coverage of the entire corridor including dark ships, defeating the "authorized route" premise, or (b) Iran struck a known Qatari state vessel deliberately, not a random targeting error.

MarineTraffic data shows Wedyan's last position was in the Gulf on July 3; Al Rekayyat had picked up LNG at Ras Laffan earlier in the month. Neither vessel's transponder was active at time of strike per Kpler and MarineTraffic records cited by CNN and Business Times.

Qatar's LNG exports are central to the post-war economic recovery narrative. Ras Laffan has been ramping up since the June 28 MOU signing. A strike on a Nakilat vessel carrying Qatari state cargo — days before Khamenei's burial and three weeks after signing the MOU — is a direct message to Doha: your government is not protected by the agreement you signed.

UKMTO confirmed a tanker struck east of Limah, Oman — outside the narrowest portion of the strait. Axios confirmed Iranian missiles, citing two US officials. The WSJ published the engine room distress call: "Engine room fire and full of smoke. Unable to assess further damage. All crew are safe and mustered on the starboard side."
analysis:
The documentary record — the MOU, the IRGC radio warning, the authorized corridor — was published and broadcast publicly. Within 72 hours it was violated by an IRGC strike on a vessel that did exactly what the MOU said would keep it safe. This is not ambiguity. The MOU's central security guarantee — that following the authorized corridor would protect commercial vessels — was falsified by Iran's own missiles within three days of Khamenei's funeral.

The named-vessel and named-operator combination (Al Rekayyat / Nakilat / Qatar flag) is more specific than any prior IRGC Hormuz strike in June. The June 27 IRGC Article 5 claim targeted "US deployment sites" generically. The June 28 Ali Al Salem strikes hit Bahraini and unspecified vessels. This strike hits a specific Qatari state-owned LNG vessel on a specific mission: loading cargo at Ras Laffan, the world's largest LNG terminal, and transiting the corridor Iran itself declared safe.

The engine room strike — "port side at the top of the engine room" — is a disabling strike, not a sinking attempt. The IRGC wanted the vessel immobile, not destroyed. A disabling strike on a Qatari state-owned LNG vessel is a different signal than a random commercial hit: it is a demonstration that Iran can reach any vessel in the Gulf regardless of what agreements are in place, and that the MOU's security architecture is contingent on Iran's choice, not its absence of capability.

The 4.1 percent European gas price rise is the economic lever Iran is pulling. Qatar's LNG is the marginal supplier to Europe. A strike that demonstrates the supply chain is vulnerable — even without disrupting flows — moves the market. The strike is as much about signaling to European energy markets as to Doha or Washington.
verdict: The OSINT finding is the documentary contradiction: Iran declared an authorized corridor safe, warned that vessels following it would be protected, then struck a vessel on that corridor while it was dark. The load-bearing question is whether Iran has surveillance sufficient to identify dark ships in the authorized corridor — which would mean the corridor was never safe, and the MOU's central security guarantee was fiction from the start. The economic signal — 4.1 percent European gas — is Iran demonstrating it can move energy markets regardless of diplomatic agreements.
